comment: Baseline rules embedded into the Sentinel binary via include_bytes!. The eventual remote rules file at rules-v1.json will follow the same schema. Rules can be added here without code changes; behavior (conditions, apply, state checks) is restricted to the named kinds defined in Rust.

rules.title: Enable Windows Game Mode
rules.description: Game Mode tells Windows to prioritize the foreground game, deprioritize background updates, and pause Windows Update reboots while you're playing.

rules.title: Trim Windows visual effects
rules.description: Animations, transparency, and shadow effects look nice but cost a few percent of GPU and CPU. Setting the 'best performance' preset turns most off; some apply immediately, the rest on your next sign-in.
rules.impact: Snappier UI · slightly higher in-game FPS
rules.downside: UI looks more utilitarian — no fade animations.

rules.title: Disable mouse acceleration ('Enhance pointer precision')
rules.description: Windows applies a non-linear acceleration curve to mouse movement by default — the same physical motion produces different cursor distances depending on how fast you move. Off = 1:1 movement, which is what every competitive shooter expects and what aim-training builds muscle memory around.
rules.impact: Consistent aim · predictable flicks · removes a hidden variable
rules.downside: If you've gotten used to acceleration for desktop use, the cursor will feel slower at first — you may want to bump DPI / sensitivity to compensate.

rules.title: Disable Game Bar and Game DVR
rules.description: Game Bar's background capture and Game DVR (Windows' built-in recording layer) add CPU and disk overhead in every running game whether you use them or not. Most users have third-party capture (OBS, ShadowPlay, AMD ReLive) and never touch Windows' version. Turning it off frees up resources.
rules.impact: Lower background overhead in every game
rules.downside: You'll lose the Win+G overlay and Windows' built-in clip recording.

rules.title: Disable Windows telemetry (DiagTrack)
rules.description: DiagTrack ('Connected User Experiences and Telemetry') runs in the background sending usage and diagnostic data to Microsoft. Disabling it has no functional impact on day-to-day use but does mean some of the data Windows uses to detect crashes and roll back broken updates won't be sent.
rules.impact: Less background network traffic · less idle CPU · privacy
rules.downside: Windows feedback submissions and automatic update-rollback diagnostics rely on this service. Most users never notice.

rules.title: Disable Windows Search indexer (HDD-only systems)
rules.description: On systems with only spinning hard drives, the Windows Search service (WSearch) constantly indexes files and causes meaningful disk thrash that you can hear and feel. On NVMe / SSD systems the indexing cost is small and the speed savings are real, so Sentinel hides this recommendation entirely unless every detected drive is an HDD.
rules.impact: Lower idle disk activity · less HDD thrash · ~50–150 MB RAM back
rules.downside: Start menu / File Explorer search becomes slower and less complete — it falls back to live filesystem walking instead of pre-built indexes. You can re-enable any time.

rules.title: Disable Nagle's Algorithm (advanced — TCP-heavy games only)
rules.description: Nagle's Algorithm batches small TCP packets together to save bandwidth at the cost of a few ms of latency. This tweak is widely recommended in gaming guides, but most modern games run over UDP, not TCP — disabling Nagle does nothing for them. It can help in games that genuinely use TCP for gameplay traffic (some MMORPGs, certain older titles, some emulators), and is otherwise advanced-mode territory.
rules.impact: Lower latency in games that actually use TCP for gameplay traffic
rules.downside: Marginally more network overhead. For UDP-based games (which is most of them today), this does nothing.
rules.applies_to_template: Active network adapter — verify your specific game uses TCP before enabling

rules.title: Disable USB Selective Suspend (AC power)
rules.description: Windows lets the USB stack put your peripherals into a low-power state when idle. For wired gaming mice, keyboards, headsets, and USB audio interfaces this can cause micro-stutters at the worst moments (right when you click after a brief idle). Sentinel disables this only for AC power — laptop battery behavior stays exactly as Windows configured it.
rules.impact: Removes a known cause of mouse/keyboard micro-stutter and audio crackle right after idle
rules.downside: Slightly higher idle USB power draw on AC. Battery behavior unchanged.
rules.applies_to_template: Active power plan, AC profile only

rules.title: Disable PCIe Link State Power Management (AC power)
rules.description: Windows lets PCIe devices (your GPU, NVMe SSDs, sound cards) negotiate down to a lower power state when idle. Coming back out of that low-power state during gameplay introduces tens-to-hundreds of microseconds of latency at unpredictable moments — most notably as a stutter when assets stream in. Sentinel disables this only for AC; battery behavior is preserved.
rules.impact: Removes a documented cause of stutter during asset streaming and GPU/NVMe wake-up
rules.downside: Slightly higher idle PCIe power draw on AC. Battery behavior unchanged.
rules.applies_to_template: Active power plan, AC profile only — affects GPU and NVMe SSD link states

rules.title: Disable Energy Efficient Ethernet on the gaming NIC
rules.description: Energy Efficient Ethernet (EEE / Green Ethernet / similar names) lets your wired NIC dim down when traffic is idle. The downside is a small but real latency variance every time the link wakes back up — the kind of thing you feel as inconsistent ping in competitive shooters. Sentinel only modifies adapters that are wired Ethernet, link-up, and have the property exposed by their driver. Wi-Fi, virtual, and Bluetooth adapters are left alone.
rules.impact: More consistent latency on the wired gaming NIC; reduces ping variance
rules.downside: Slightly higher idle network power draw on the adapter (a fraction of a watt).
rules.applies_to_template: Active wired Ethernet adapter with an EEE-shaped property exposed by the driver

rules.title: Memory Integrity / VBS is active — measurable FPS cost in some games
rules.description: Memory Integrity (also called HVCI) and the broader Virtualization-Based Security stack run kernel-mode code under a hypervisor for stronger isolation. This is excellent against certain malware classes (DMA attacks, exploits via vulnerable signed drivers, kernel-mode rootkits), but it has a measurable cost in some workloads — including a handful of games, where it can shave 5–15% off frame rate in CPU-bound scenes. Sentinel surfaces this as an advisory, NOT a one-click apply: disabling Memory Integrity weakens real security guarantees, so the choice belongs to you, not to a default. If you decide it's worth it for your competitive use, the switch is in Settings → Privacy & security → Windows Security → Device security → Core isolation details → Memory integrity.
rules.impact: Restoring 5–15% FPS in CPU-bound scenes if you choose to disable
rules.downside: Real security regression: lower protection against DMA attacks, vulnerable-signed-driver exploits, and kernel-mode rootkits. Some kernel-mode anti-cheat (Valorant Vanguard, some Easy Anti-Cheat / BattlEye configurations) may also require it.
rules.applies_to_template: Memory Integrity / VBS is currently engaged on this machine

rules.title: Add your game install folders to Defender's exclusion list
rules.description: Microsoft Defender real-time scanning hits game folders harder than most other paths: large updates trigger heavy I/O during patching, shader caches get rebuilt and rewritten constantly, and asset streaming during play hits files Defender has already scanned. Adding your game install roots (Steam library folders, Epic's installation directory, Riot, Battle.net, etc.) to Defender's exclusion list removes that overhead. Sentinel won't auto-apply this — exclusion is a security-tradeoff decision you should make once you understand it, not a default. The control is in Settings → Privacy & security → Windows Security → Virus & threat protection → Manage settings → Exclusions.
rules.impact: Smoother game installs and updates · faster shader compilation · fewer mid-game stutters from background scans
rules.downside: Files in the excluded folders are not scanned in real-time. Only exclude folders that ONLY contain game data you trust — never your Downloads folder, never your Desktop, never anywhere you save attachments.
rules.applies_to_template: All Windows installs running Microsoft Defender

rules.title: Check that Variable Refresh Rate is on (G-SYNC / FreeSync)
rules.description: If your monitor supports G-SYNC, G-SYNC Compatible, or FreeSync (and most modern gaming monitors do), Variable Refresh Rate eliminates the screen tearing you'd otherwise get from frame rates that don't match the panel's refresh rate. It also makes frame-rate dips feel less jarring because the panel resyncs each frame instead of holding stale content. Two switches need to be on for it to work: Windows ('Variable refresh rate' in Settings → System → Display → Graphics → Default graphics settings) AND your GPU vendor's control panel (NVIDIA Control Panel → Set up G-SYNC, or AMD Adrenalin → Display → AMD FreeSync). Sentinel doesn't auto-apply because monitor and GPU compatibility varies, and on a small number of older displays VRR can cause flicker — the user should verify it works on their specific hardware.
rules.impact: Eliminates tearing · smoother feel during frame-rate dips · no input-lag cost when configured correctly
rules.downside: On some panels VRR can cause brightness flicker, especially in dark scenes with big FPS swings. If you see flicker, turn VRR off for that monitor.
rules.applies_to_template: Verify monitor + GPU + Windows + vendor control panel all have VRR enabled

rules.title: Disable audio enhancements on your gaming output device
rules.description: Windows audio 'enhancements' (Loudness Equalization, Bass Boost, Virtual Surround, Room Correction, Speaker Fill, and similar driver-side effects) sit between the game and your output device. They add a few milliseconds of latency and, more importantly, change the spatial cues competitive shooters rely on for footstep direction. For movies, music, and immersive single-player, the enhancements may sound better and are worth keeping. Sentinel surfaces this as an advisory: open Sound Settings → click your active output device → Device properties → Additional device properties → Enhancements tab → check 'Disable all enhancements' (or 'Disable all sound effects' depending on Windows version). The Spatial sound dropdown on the same screen — Windows Sonic / Dolby Atmos for Headphones — is a separate decision and many competitive players keep one of those on.
rules.impact: Tighter audio latency · accurate spatial positioning · footstep direction stays where the game put it
rules.downside: Music and movies may lose punch (no bass boost, no loudness EQ). If you mainly play single-player cinematics, leaving enhancements on is reasonable.
rules.applies_to_template: Active default output device — change per device if you switch between headphones and speakers

rules.title: Check that your most-played games live on your fastest drive
rules.description: Big modern games (Call of Duty Warzone, Baldur's Gate 3, Cyberpunk 2077, Final Fantasy XIV) stream tens of gigabytes during loading screens and map transitions. On an HDD this turns 8-second loads into 45-second loads and causes mid-match texture pop-in; on a SATA SSD it's tolerable; on an NVMe SSD it's near-instant. The right move is usually NOT 'upgrade your drive' but 'move the 2-3 games you actually play to the fastest drive you already own.' Steam: right-click the game in your library → Properties → Installed Files → Move install folder. Epic: Library → ⋯ → Move. Battle.net: Settings → Game Install/Update → drive picker (then verify integrity). Most launchers move the install without re-downloading. Once moved, the rest of the library on the slower drive can stay there.
rules.impact: Map and asset loads measured in seconds instead of tens of seconds · less texture pop-in mid-match · less file-I/O competition between your active game and a background launcher update
rules.downside: Time investment (5-30 min per game during the move) and you need enough free space on the target drive. Validate the move worked before deleting the source folder if your launcher leaves both.
rules.applies_to_template: Move competitive / most-played titles to your fastest drive; leave large single-player libraries on slower drives
